title: Error Propagation & Significant Figures Rules
notes:
Gateway of Knowledge

Often the certainty in a measured value is not specified explicitly. In such cases, the uncertainty is generally assumed to be one or two units in the last digit specified. For example, if a length is given as 6.2 cm, the uncertainty is assumed to be about 0.1 cm or 0.2 cm — that is, the value is read as 6.2 ± 0.1 cm or 6.2 ± 0.2 cm. If we instead assumed an uncertainty of 0.01 cm, we would be claiming the value lies between 6.19 cm and 6.21 cm, when we really believe it lies between 6.1 cm and 6.3 cm.

Error in Sum and Difference

Let x = a + b. Then Δx = ±(Δa + Δb).

Similarly, let x = a − b. Then Δx = ±(Δa + Δb).

In both addition and subtraction, the absolute errors add up.

Error in Product and Division

Let x = a × b. Then Δx/x = ±(Δa/a + Δb/b)

Let x = a/b. Then Δx/x = ±(Δa/a + Δb/b)

In both multiplication and division, the fractional (relative) errors add up.

Example: Calculate uncertainty in percentage for the measurement 3.22

Generally, error in a measured value is not specified explicitly, so the error is assumed to be one or two units in the last digit specified. For the measurement 3.22, the uncertainty is therefore taken as 3.22 ± 0.01.

Measured value with uncertainty = 3.22 ± 0.01

% Uncertainty = Uncertainty/Measured value × 100% = 0.01/3.22 × 100% = 0.31%

1.10 Significant Figures (Digits)

In physics there are limits to the accuracy of measurement and its reliability. The simple way of expressing this reliability is by using significant figures. The number of digits (figures) in a given number which we are reasonably sure about are called significant figures. The more significant figures specified, the greater the precision implied.

For example, if the diameter of a rod is measured and its value is found to be 0.004 mm, we feel that 4 is a reasonable value but we are not sure of the next figure. So we have indicated only one significant figure.

Rules to Determine the Number of Significant Figures

  1. All non-zero digits are significant. For example, 2365 has four significant figures.
  2. Zeros between two non-zero digits are significant. For example, 1003 has four significant figures.
  3. Zeros to the right of the last non-zero digit are not significant unless they are followed by a decimal point. For example, 1300 has two significant figures, but 1300. has four.
  4. Zeros to the right of a decimal point but to the left of a non-zero digit are not significant. For example, 0.00356 has three significant figures.
  5. Zeros to the right of a decimal point and also to the right of a non-zero digit are significant. For example, 0.07600 has four significant figures.
  6. All zeros to the right of the last non-zero digit after the decimal point are significant. For example, 4.00, 4.000 and 4.0000 have three, four and five significant figures respectively.
  7. Zeros to the right of the last non-zero digit are significant only if they come from a measurement.
  8. Exact numbers have infinite significant figures. For example, in the area of a square, A = 4 × side, the 4 is an exact number and has infinite significant figures.
  9. Addition and subtraction: the result is rounded to the same decimal place as the quantity with the fewest decimal places. For example, the sum of 103.9 kg + 2.10 kg + 0.319 kg is 106.319 kg, which is rounded to 106.3 kg (one decimal place).
  10. Multiplication and division: the result keeps as many significant figures as the original number with the fewest significant figures.
